$comment: Nub-IA model tiers. Patterns are case-insensitive regexes matched against `provider/id`, tried in order within each provider; providers are tried in providerPriority order (the provider already serving the session goes first). Among the models one pattern matches, the newest version wins (so gpt-6.1-sol beats gpt-6-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5 beats claude-sonnet-5), then the cheapest output price. Claude is preferred where a provider offers both families; for OpenAI (`openai` = the ChatGPT/Codex subscription login in Pi 1.x, `openai-codex` = the id Pi marks as legacy; both treated alike) only the newest generation (gpt-6.x) is used, with gpt-5.5/5.6 as a last resort when a provider lacks gpt-6. Open-weight providers (opencode-go, nvidia) rank by capability/cost within their own catalogs; llama.cpp (local GGUF files, arbitrary ids) matches whatever is loaded, newest/largest-numbered first. Edit here to change the team's routing; no code change needed. A repository can override this file at .pi/nub-ia/model-tiers.json.
$budget: Optional spend ceiling, off by default. Example: "budget": { "dailyUsd": 20, "sessionUsd": 5, "onExceed": "warn" }. Spend is what Pi prices per assistant message; the day total is shared by every session of this machine (<configHome>/metrics/spend-<date>.json). onExceed "warn" notifies once and shows the line in the Status Router block; "degrade" also routes strong/strong-alt → balanced → fast until the limit resets. A repository's .pi/nub-ia/model-tiers.json can only tighten this (lower limits, degrade over warn). Meaningful with pay-per-use providers (Bedrock, NVIDIA, OpenCode Go); for subscriptions (Copilot, OpenAI) Pi's per-message cost is nominal, not what the team pays, and the daily ledger is per machine.
$allowlist: Optional. "allowedProviders": ["amazon-bedrock"] restricts the whole session (router tiers and manual /model alike) to those providers; "deniedModels": ["gpt-5-mini"] are regexes against provider/id that are never used. A repository's .pi/nub-ia/model-tiers.json can only narrow these (intersection of providers, union of denied patterns). Typical use: a client that forbids sending code to anything but the company's Bedrock account.
